blocks.text: **Lateral elbow tendinopathy**, commonly called tennis elbow, is a load-related tendon problem at the outer elbow where the wrist and finger extensor muscles attach to the **lateral epicondyle**, a bony point on the outside of the elbow. The extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) tendon is most often involved [Ref - to verify]. The condition is not mainly an inflammation, so the older terms lateral epicondylitis and tendinitis are less preferred.

It is most common between about 35 and 55 years old and often follows repeated gripping, lifting or wrist extension work, such as manual work, computer or tool use, and racket sports. Many people have never played tennis [Ref - to verify]. Most cases settle over months, even with limited treatment, but a share have symptoms for a year or more [Ref - to verify].

items: Pain on the outer elbow that may spread down the forearm.
Pain with gripping, lifting, shaking hands, turning a screwdriver or a door handle, carrying a bag with the palm down, and using a mouse.
Tenderness over the lateral epicondyle or just below it.
Reduced and painful grip strength. Elbow range of movement is usually normal.
Gradual onset is typical.

rows: Where exactly is the pain: outer elbow, forearm, or deep behind the joint?
Which activities provoke it: gripping, lifting, typing, racket sports?
Has your work, hobby or training load changed?
Any neck pain, arm numbness or tingling?
Any locking, catching, or giving way in the elbow?
Any fever, swelling, or multiple painful joints?
What do you need to be able to do?

items: Observe the elbow and forearm for swelling, wasting and posture.
Palpate the lateral epicondyle, the common extensor tendon, the radial head and the muscle belly.
Elbow, forearm and wrist range of movement.
Resisted wrist extension and finger extension.
Grip strength, ideally pain-free grip strength compared with the other side.
Special tests (Section E).
Cervical and neurological screen of the arm.
Radial tunnel screen (Section E).

blocks.text: Honest note: tennis elbow is a clinical diagnosis. The tests below reproduce familiar pain at the tendon but do not prove a tear or measure tendon damage. Imaging is rarely needed [Ref - to verify].
E1. Palpation of the lateral epicondyle

rows: Sitting with the elbow bent to about 90 degrees and supported
Press on the lateral epicondyle and the area just in front of and below it, where the extensor tendon attaches
Localised tenderness that reproduces the familiar pain
Tenderness is also present with other conditions, so combine with load tests

blocks.text: E2. Cozen test (resisted wrist extension)

rows: Load the wrist extensors to see whether the outer elbow pain is reproduced
Sitting; elbow bent to about 90 degrees, forearm pronated, fist closed
Beside the patient, one hand supports the elbow and palpates the lateral epicondyle, the other hand holds the back of the patient's hand
The patient extends the wrist and radially deviates it against the therapist's resistance, while the therapist keeps palpating the epicondyle
Sharp familiar pain at the lateral epicondyle
Not specific; accuracy is limited [Ref - to verify]
Resisting at the fingers, not the hand; applying force too quickly

blocks.text: E3. Mill test (passive stretch)

rows: Passively flex the wrist fully while keeping the elbow straight and the forearm pronated

blocks.text: E4. Maudsley test (resisted middle finger extension)

rows: Sitting, elbow extended, forearm pronated, fingers extended
The patient extends the middle finger against resistance applied to the top of the finger

blocks.text: E5. Pain-free grip strength

Use a handheld dynamometer. Test grip with the elbow extended and with the elbow bent, and note the level at which pain starts. Record pain-free grip and compare with the other side. This is a useful baseline and progress measure [Ref - to verify; avoid quoting norm values].
E6. Radial tunnel check

The radial tunnel is a passage near the supinator muscle where the posterior interosseous nerve can be compressed. Palpate over the radial tunnel (about 3 to 5 cm below the lateral epicondyle, over the supinator) and ask the patient to resist supination with the elbow straight, and to extend the middle finger against resistance. Pain in that area, rather than over the epicondyle, suggests radial tunnel syndrome. The two conditions can occur together [Ref - to verify].
E7. Outcome measures
Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation (PRTEE) and a 0 to 10 pain scale [Ref - to verify].

rows: Deeper, more distal forearm pain, pain on resisted supination or middle finger extension, little epicondyle tenderness
Nerve-focused care, medical review if persistent
History of dislocation or injury, clicking, apprehension

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Fall or injury with swelling, inability to straighten or rotate the arm
Hot, red, swollen elbow with fever
Progressive weakness or wasting, numbness in the hand or fingers
Constant night pain, weight loss, a lump
Multiple swollen painful joints with morning stiffness
Sudden loss of grip with a gap at the tendon
Chest pain, sweating, breathlessness with arm pain

sections.title: H. Working diagnosis and decision pathway

items: Any emergency or urgent flag? **Yes:** act as in Section G.
Neck or nerve source suspected? Use the cervical or nerve pathway.
Outer elbow pain, epicondyle tenderness, pain on resisted wrist or middle finger extension, normal elbow range? **Yes:** working diagnosis is lateral elbow tendinopathy.
Pain over the radial tunnel or posterior interosseous nerve signs? Consider radial tunnel syndrome, alone or together.
Begin education, load management and progressive loading.
If there is no improvement after a full trial, review the diagnosis and consider medical options.

rows: May give short-term pain relief and improve pain-free grip [Ref - to verify]
Pain on gripping that eases with the technique
Sitting with the elbow extended; the therapist applies a lateral glide to the forearm just below the elbow, the patient grips, and repeat several times
The technique does not reduce pain immediately, or pain increases
Gentle sustained pressure on the muscle belly, not heavy pressure on the tender tendon

blocks.text: **Preferred starting choice:** education, load management and progressive loading. Manual therapy is optional for short-term relief, and the effect is generally small [Ref - to verify]. Do not use deep friction massage as the main treatment. Do not claim to break up scar tissue.

sections.title: J. Exercise prescription (example starting plan, not universal)

blocks.text: **Principle:** tendon loading is the core treatment. A short period of isometric holds to calm pain, then progressive strengthening of the wrist extensors, grip and the whole arm. Several exercise types appear helpful, and adherence matters most [Ref - to verify].

rows: Sit with the forearm on a table, palm down; the patient holds the wrist in extension while resisted lightly by the other hand
5 holds of 30 to 45 seconds, once or twice a day
Wrist extension with a light dumbbell, slow tempo; supination and pronation with a hammer or weight
Raise the wrist for about 3 seconds, lower for about 3 seconds
Heavier wrist extension, reverse curls, towel or putty grip, farmer's carry
Pain stays at about 3 to 4 out of 10 or less and no flare the next day
Racket or tool work simulation, lifting tasks, return to sport

blocks.text: **Eccentric exercise with a flexible rubber bar (twist exercise):** some trials suggest benefit [Ref - to verify]. It is optional, and the patient should find it comfortable.
**Symptom rule:** pain up to about 3 to 4 out of 10 during exercise that settles within 24 hours is acceptable. Pain that stays higher into the next day means reduce load.

**Load management and ergonomics:** reduce, rather than stop, painful gripping and lifting. Change tool handles to a larger grip, keep the wrist neutral, lift with the palm up when possible, use both hands, take breaks, and adjust mouse and keyboard setup.
**Bracing:** a forearm counterforce strap just below the elbow may reduce pain with gripping for some people in the short term [Ref - to verify]. Wrist splints are not routine.

**Medical options (decided by doctors):** corticosteroid injection may reduce pain in the short term, but studies show worse outcomes at longer follow-up (about a year) compared with waiting or physiotherapy, and higher recurrence [Ref - to verify]. Platelet-rich plasma injections do not show consistent benefit [Ref - to verify]. Surgery is rare and for persistent severe cases.

items: **Visit 1:** screen flags, neck and nerve sources, explain the condition and its usual course, set goals.
**Early:** reduce painful gripping, start isometrics, consider a strap and manual therapy for comfort.
**Middle:** progressive strengthening for about 8 to 12 weeks [Ref - to verify].
**Late:** return to full work, sport and gripping tasks; maintenance exercise.
**If no improvement after about 3 months of consistent care:** review diagnosis, consider radial tunnel or cervical sources, and specialist options.

blocks.text: Record pain-free grip strength, pain on a 0 to 10 scale during a standard task, PRTEE, pain on resisted wrist extension and the patient's function goal.

rows: No improvement after about 12 weeks of consistent care

blocks.text: **Case:** A 46-year-old mechanic has 4 months of right outer elbow pain when gripping tools and lifting parts. Tenderness is at the lateral epicondyle. Cozen test reproduces his pain, and grip strength is lower on the right with pain. Elbow range is full. Neck and neurological screens are normal. No red flags.

**Working diagnosis:** lateral elbow tendinopathy. **Plan:** education, change tool grip and lifting technique, isometric then progressive wrist extension and grip loading over about 12 weeks, optional forearm strap, reassess every 3 to 4 weeks, and avoid steroid injection as a first step.
**Questions and answers**

items: Why is a corticosteroid injection not a first choice? It may give short-term relief, but studies show worse results and more recurrence at about one year [Ref - to verify].

How do you tell tennis elbow from radial tunnel syndrome? Tennis elbow is tender at the epicondyle, while radial tunnel pain is deeper and more distal, with pain on resisted supination or middle finger extension.
Why test the neck? Cervical root problems can refer pain to the outer elbow and forearm, and treating the elbow alone would not help.
Why measure pain-free grip? It is a simple, repeatable baseline of function that shows progress.
Why reduce rather than stop gripping tasks? Complete rest lowers load capacity, while gradual loading rebuilds it.
**Initial approach:** education, load management and progressive loading.
**Justifying findings:** outer elbow pain, epicondyle tenderness, pain on resisted wrist extension, normal elbow range.
**Priority:** tendon capacity and grip function.
**Manual therapy:** optional short-term adjunct.
**Exercise:** isometrics, wrist extension strengthening, grip and functional loading.
**Modalities:** limited role.
**Tell the patient:** common, usually improves over months, exercise is the core treatment.
**Avoid:** deep friction, complete rest, early steroid injection.
**Measure:** pain-free grip, PRTEE, task pain.
**If no improvement:** specialist review.
**Referral triggers:** Section G.
**Discharge:** function restored with a maintenance plan.

blocks.text: **Assumptions:** adult, no fracture, no cervical or nerve cause.

items: **Can be tested:** whether exercise, bracing or manual therapy improve pain and grip; the effect of injections over time.
**Hypotheses:** that loading improves tendon capacity and changes pain processing.
**Future questions:** the best exercise dose, and which patients benefit from shockwave or surgery.

blocks.text: Evidence not graded until references are verified.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Explain tennis elbow as a load problem.
Perform palpation, Cozen, Mill and Maudsley tests and state their limits.
Separate it from radial tunnel syndrome and cervical referral.
Build a staged loading program.
